800: I can tell you what happened two thousand years ago exactly. Ask me what I had for lunch, though.
801: I began today's lecture in one century and somehow ended in another. This happens to me often.
802: I know the names of a hundred forgotten kings. I do not know where I left my keys. This is the trade.
803: A student asked what year it is. I gave them four possible answers, all from the distant past.
804: I love the past. It is finished, it holds still, and it never once asks me to check my messages.
805: My lectures have a clear beginning and, eventually, an end. What happens in the middle surprises us both.
806: I brought one small note to class and spoke for two hours. The note said only one word: begin.
807: The old days were full of drama and grand speeches. I belong in them. I was simply born a few thousand years late.
808: I can describe an ancient feast in delicious detail. My own kitchen remains a total mystery to me.
809: Students set alarms so I know when to stop. I have taught right through several of them. Gently.
810: I got so lost in a tangent today that I forgot the question. It was a wonderful tangent, though.
811: I hold the whole sweep of the ages in my head. Today's date, however, keeps slipping right out.
812: I told a story about a very old bridge for forty minutes. The bridge fell down long ago. I miss it.
813: A child asked if I was alive back then. I said no. Then I paused a very long, thoughtful while.
814: I could talk about a single old coin until everyone quietly leaves. Some days I test this theory.
815: The past is my whole world. The present keeps arriving on schedule, and I keep being politely surprised by it.
816: I answered a short question with a long journey through three empires. The student wanted the time.
817: I remember battles from a thousand years ago. I do not remember starting this sentence. Where was I.
818: Every fact reminds me of another fact. That is why my classes end when the building closes, not before.
819: I once assigned a short reading and lectured on it for a month. It was, I felt, barely enough time.
820: Every airport hallway looks the same and leads somewhere different. Pick one and start walking, detective.
821: The plane landed, your suitcase landed a little later, and your hopes landed somewhere in between.
822: Welcome to arrivals. Everyone here looks like they know exactly where they're going. Blend in.
823: You slept for six minutes on the flight and woke up ready to solve everything. Bold.
824: Fresh runway, fresh clues, and one foot that's been asleep since takeoff. Wake it up.
825: Boarding now: you, a suitcase, and a plan that fits neatly on the back of a napkin.
826: The seatbelt light went off, and so did your last good idea. You'll find another.
827: A brand-new city, and it has absolutely no idea you're here to fix everything. Surprise.
828: You stepped off the plane and your legs remembered how walking works about halfway down the hallway.
829: New skyline, new streets, new chance to walk confidently in the wrong direction.
830: The flight had one tiny pillow and big ideas about legroom. You survived both.
831: You're here! Wherever here is. Somebody wave. Nobody's waving. That's fine, you're busy.
832: Buckle up. The snacks are small, the flight is long, and your patience is somewhere in the overhead bin.
833: Another landing survived. Your knuckles can let go of the armrest now. Gently. There you go.
834: The doors opened and a hundred strangers all decided to leave at exactly the same moment. You among them.
835: You packed light, thought hard, and still can't remember which pocket you swore you put the tickets in.
836: Somewhere out there is a thief. Somewhere closer is a very long line for the bathroom.
837: You arrived a little crumpled and a lot curious. One of those will smooth out on the walk over.
838: You landed with a suitcase, a hunch, and the quiet confidence of someone who mostly slept.
839: The plane finally stopped moving, which is your body's official signal to start paying attention again.
